You write quote, the consumer case for updating and better enforcing the nation's antitrust laws is straightforward. It will bring down prices by giving the citizens of this country some much needed leverage and it will give Americans more choice. So my question, Senator, if Americans didn't buy their goods on Amazon, would prices be cheaper? But right now you've got an Amazon company that does give people some deals. And one of the things you've seen suit history is monopolies will underprice many times to get people out of the market, then eventually the prices creep up. And I can't tell you when that moment in time will happen, but that is what has tended to happen. And this doesn't mean again that you get rid of Amazon. It means that you put conditions in, things like you can't self-preference your own products. which Google has been proven to do in the past as well. That is an unfair advantage. You're using the information you have. You have to allow access. I think the best example of this right now is the app stores where Google and Apple are basically saying to companies like Spotify and Tile and Match.com, all of whom testified before our hearing that Senator Lee and I had a few weeks ago They have to pay up to 30% of what they get off of the revenue, off of people going to their app. Other companies don't. And there was a really interesting exchange between Senator Lee and the Apple witness about why this would be that they get to pick and choose who has to pay 30% and who doesn't. And so all of this to me cries out for some rules of the road because monopolies will do what monopolies want to do and it hurts people eventually for price it hurts them from innovation and it hurts them even when it comes to wages and the like. So let me ask you about Target, which is a corporation in your home state has a market cap of 106 billion, sells everything from books to bathing suits to electronics, and it even sells its own products that compete with products from other suppliers. People love Target. Would you be inclined to try to evaluate and stop a merger between Target and another large retailer? Well, if it hurts competition, yes, I think it goes into any. It doesn't matter to me if it's a hometown company or not. The other day someone compared it to me to like App Store, they said to me, well, what's the difference between Apple having an App Store and Target? They also make money off of things sold in their store. Well, the difference is that if you want to sell on an App Store, It's the only game in town for Apple phones. You have to go to Apple for non Apple phones. You got to go to Google. If you're in the middle of Target and you don't like a price, you can go you can look up on your phone. You can find another price and you can go over there. It's a way different situation in a competitive market versus a non competitive market. But if the question is about, am I somehow afraid of taking on any companies? No, I'm not. My issue is Congress has been afraid to do this. We haven't gotten one thing done. I have 25 ideas of things we could move forward on, and all right now it is a bunch of talk. A couple of points on that. So Google, for example, has purchased a firm at the rate of one every 18 days over the last decade. The five tech companies, Facebook, Google, Microsoft, Amazon, and Apple are now worth a combined $8 trillion. The combined market share of the big five companies has soared even more during the COVID pandemic as people have relied increasingly on technology. Can you Senator give us an example of a business practice employed by one of those companies that you consider harmful to consumers? Sure. So I think the business practice of, let's say, Facebook, deciding they just want to bring and buy up every small competitor in their area. I think that's harmful to competitors. And let me say why. First of all, we know it's true. We have the emails as Exhibit A from Mark Zuckerberg, in which he said, I'd rather buy than compete. This came out in Sicilini's Hearings in the House. And he also said, these brands may be nascent, and then he said the magic words, but they could be disruptive to us. So he bought them because he wanted to make sure they didn't become disruptive to them. So what does this mean for consumers? Well, maybe Instagram and WhatsApp would have developed the misinformation bells and whistles and the privacy bells and whistles that would have put us in a much better place. And people would have gravitated over to those platforms. We will never know that because they were bought out by the big guy on the block. And that is Facebook. When you look at the app stores, We won't know about all the companies that have come to me that don't want their names known, that they've had to pull back on things. They are never even allowed to blossom. They can start up, but their only way to really go up is by being bought out by the big guys. That is not capitalism as we want it to work. You write that the Obama administration's allowance of multiple tech mergers and apparent lack of interest in full-scale tech investigations allowed big tech to get, well, even bigger. How would you grade the Obama administration's antitrust policies, especially with respect to big tech? I will say that they had some major issues there and I am not afraid to point that out in the book. I have an interview in there from Cara Swisher in interviewing James Burling, you know, in which he was honest. He said, look, when I look back at Facebook's purchase of WhatsApp and Instagram, now we should have done something. And I think people were so enamored with tech at the time. You know, they said, trust us and everyone believed them and they were great American companies employing people. That's all true. So they just kind of let it go. You add to that the sophistication of these companies. And the fact that Congress, as we know from some of the questioning, didn't really weren't able to cope with it. You've got multiple problems in them taking it on. Now we've reached a different point because we have seen the bad. We have seen the misinformation on vaccines and the like. We have seen the privacy and the data mining that goes on where we are nothing but profit centers. And so what are we going to do? Just step back and say, this is too complicated. We're not going to do something. I don't buy it. And I thought the app hearing that Senator Lee and I had just shows that we actually are onto this now. And we are ready to do some sensible, rational things to take this on. Take a look at some of the statements from you and your colleagues during that recent subcommittee hearing in April. Just because a company creates a successful, innovative business that consumers like doesn't give it a free pass to harm, competition, or ignore our antitrust laws. Google and Apple are here to defend the patently indefensible. Apple is happy to Jerry Rig the Rules. We've got witnesses here telling us that they're, um, that they're scared. It's fair to say that both sides of the aisle are uncomfortable with the growing power in big tech. Does bipartisan consensus extend to finding solutions? It has to. And I think this is the year we're going to find out whether or not it does. There's been a lot of talk, but the time is to get things done. And I know that Senator Grassley has devoted to this, as is actually Senator Blackburn, in moving this bill forward. Republicans are constantly coming up to me on everything from cattle prices to browsers to what's happening with pharma. And so we are going to have to break down what I think will have to do my bill because I don't believe in monopolies. I'm willing to break it up into sections that we have Republican support on and keep pushing through different things. And I was so pleased with that hearing because yes, we have different strong differences of opinions about Why we have problems in this country and they tend to go on this content issue and liberals work at tech and that kind of stuff. I just think we're not going to get consensus on that so and I don't agree with them so let's move forward on the stuff we do agree on which is how do we stop exclusionary conduct and how do we change the merger standing going forward. And how do we make sure the agencies are funded so they can actually do their jobs? Those are three basic things we can do. So conservative legal giant Robert Bork, who you write about in your book, appeared on Firing Line with William F. Buckley Jr. several times, his seminal book, The Antitrux Paradox. was recently re-released with a new introduction written by your colleague, Senator Mike Lee. Yeah, I know. Josh Hawley, on the other hand, the GOP Senator from Missouri has aligned himself very firmly with the Brandeisians, who take the opposite view of the Borgians when it comes to the larger antitrust debate. You, Senator, seem to be somewhere in the middle of them, which is a wild place to be. What are your guiding principles for how you approach antitrust? I have to tell you the first person that's interviewed me that actually gets this Holly Lee dichotomy in this. It's crazy. No, thank you for bringing it up. Let me start with Mike Lee. He and I are good friends. I was so glad he joined me on this App Store. We did the whole thing together. We went after Apple when they wouldn't give us a witness or questioning Google about why someone called to intimidate, get this match.com the day before the hearing to clearly try to get them not to testify. So we have disagreements on a few major issues. And one of them is I think work has done great damage to the standard of antitrust. But once again, it's an example, I find a common ground where I can find it. On Josh Hawley, I have not read his book yet. I know that he is in favor of doing something about exclusionary conduct. And I think that is important. But that all being said, if we just wait for the courts to change their mind on what they've been doing, we will be waiting 50 years, 100 years. The courts did interpret the Sherman Act and the Clayton Act in ways that allowed fractions to go forward during Teddy Roosevelt's time, even during Ronald Reagan's time, even during the AT&T breakup. Then at about that moment, Bork comes into the public light, judges start using his theories, which I don't agree with. People can read my book, and I trust to find out why. And that created the situation we're in now. I'd like to see judges all adjust as prior that have different interpretations, but I don't think we can wait around. That's why Congress has to reinterpret these laws and make very clear where we are by making some changes to make the laws as sophisticated as the economy we're in. And we also have to make sure the agencies have the funding to do their jobs under the existing laws. We can't wait on the courts. In 1980, William F. Buckley Jr. welcomed the editor of Barron's Weekly, Robert Blyver, to a discussion of called, quote, his big business out of hand. We both desire our ad iron monopoly legislation and to the extent that it's- No, you speak to yourself, Bill. Do you don't desire our monopoly? No, I think the marketplace is the most effective anti-monopoly agent I'm aware of. When I'm waiting there, Bob. Do you mean to say that I'm going to set up a rival utility company? You're not talking about a free market to begin with, Bill. Senator, how do you respond to the argument we just heard from Buckley's guest that the marketplace is the most effective way to curb monopolies? I greatly respect the marketplace. But even Adam Smith, the father of capitalism, always warned constantly about the standing army of monopolies. That's what he called them, and that we would always have to have a check and balance. That's what Buckley, what's why he's so incredulous about this, because he got it. That once you have a situation where you have one or two companies dominating, it's very hard for capitalism to work. And he wanted to work. I want it to work and that means the antitrust laws and other checks and balances. There's no incentive for a company that isn't completely market dominant to then use a bunch of their money to develop privacy regulations. Unless they're either afraid of government coming in, which is starting to happen, or they have a opponent, they have a competitor. And when you don't have the competitors doing things, then you're forcing the government to play their hand and come in. And I think we should do both things, regulate some things, and have competition. But I'm actually such a believer in competition that I would like to see that happen first. That's not happening right now because of monopolies. And I think that's what William Up Buckley was getting into. And if I could just one little slight tangential story, my dad was a calmness and he was very, very funny in a lot of his writings. And he once wrote some column for the Minneapolis paper about William F. Buckley, and he has sent him a note Buckley did that I chairs forever that said Mr. Klobuchar, the only one who is wittier than me is you. That's unbelievably high praise. Do you have that note? No, here's the thing. It was in one of my dad's books I was looking for for years, but I read it myself. That's amazing. We're going to take your word for it is good enough for the program. You've introduced your own version of this anti-monopoly legislation called the Competition and Antitrust Law Enforcement Act. And one of your proposals is to shift the burden of proof to the merging parties, to demonstrate that their merger will not violate the law. Why is that important? Because it's become harder and harder to prove up these cases. There was one 15-year period where plaintiffs won zero percentage of the time before the Supreme Court. So what I do here is for a major, major, merger saying, okay, instead of the government having to prove that this hurts competition, you have to show that it doesn't hurt competition. And it's just an acknowledgement of the sophisticated nature of the economy right now and the lack of resources on one side or the other. A decision was made by the Facebook oversight board. An outside group created by Facebook to review controversies that former President Trump should not get his Facebook and Instagram accounts back, but potentially could in the future. Now, thousands of QAnon accounts were also purged from Twitter after the Capitol insurrection. I know you're working on Section 230, and there are questions about how to regulate speech on the internet. Is de-platforming the best way to stop the spread of misinformation? Well, I think the first thing you need are rules in place that these companies, since they become God when it becomes to the internet, that they need to set forth. I've been looking at this. Of course, I didn't think Donald Trump should be on the platform. He's someone that is literally incited in insurrection, continues the lie that this election was somehow fraudulent, undermining our democracy, creating an unbelievable situation where someone is staunch conservative like Liz Cheney. is being pushed aside because of Donald Trump's lies. I think that's outrageous, not just for the Republican Party, but for our democracy. But in the end, this company is going to have to set its own rules about what they do. And when it comes to the bigger picture of are they immune, I think there should be exceptions for things like misinformation and civil rights violations. And interestingly enough, It's Mark Warner, who's a clearly moderate Democrat who made money in business in the tech sector. That is the one that's leading this effort to have some carve out for when their immunity ends. And I think that's our part of the job. But I do think it goes to show what a crazy situation we're in because of monopoly power. And again, I would like a more competition in this area. Senator AB Klomuchar, thank you for joining me on Firing Line. This was an incredibly interesting conversation, and I look forward to being on again. Thanks, Margaret. Well, welcome you anytime.

explicit_propositions.text: Teddy Roosevelt was a maverick who respected capitalism while opposing unchecked corporate power.
Teddy Roosevelt successfully prosecuted the Northern Securities Trust and broke up monopolies during his presidency.
The number of public companies in the U.S. has declined from 8,597 to fewer than 5,000 due largely to mergers and acquisitions.
Monopolistic control over key sectors—such as pharmaceuticals, telecommunications, and retail—harms consumers and reduces competition.
Senator Klobuchar opposes monopolies but supports large companies operating in competitive markets.
Facebook’s acquisition strategy, including buying potential competitors like Instagram and WhatsApp, undermines long-term innovation and competition.
Apple and Google impose a 30% fee on third-party apps in their respective app stores, which Senator Klobuchar views as exclusionary conduct.
Congress has failed to act on antitrust enforcement despite widespread concerns about market concentration.
Google acquires a company approximately every 18 days on average, contributing to reduced competition.
Senator Klobuchar co-chairs the Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Antitrust and Consumer Rights and advocates for stronger antitrust laws.

assumptions.text: A functioning market economy requires active regulation to prevent monopolistic behavior from undermining competition.
Historical precedents like Teddy Roosevelt’s trust-busting efforts provide a legitimate moral and legal foundation for modern antitrust reform.
Consumers benefit from competition, and the erosion of competition leads to higher prices, lower quality, and diminished innovation.
Corporate dominance in digital platforms enables systemic harms such as misinformation and data exploitation, which threaten democratic institutions.
Legislative action—not judicial interpretation—is necessary to update antitrust law to reflect the complexity of the modern digital economy.
Bipartisan cooperation on antitrust is possible on specific technical reforms, even if ideological divides remain on broader policy values.
Tech companies' self-preferencing practices (e.g., promoting their own products in search rankings) distort market fairness and harm smaller rivals.
The current legal framework, particularly post-Bork jurisprudence, unduly favors corporations and weakens enforcement capacity.
Public trust in institutions is undermined when a few powerful firms dominate critical infrastructure without accountability.
The existence of a 'Holly Lee dichotomy' reflects a genuine tension within conservatism regarding antitrust, suggesting space for pragmatic convergence.
